title: Metaphors We Live By
key_findings: Founding text of conceptual metaphor theory (CMT): people understand abstract domains through more concrete ones; linguistic metaphors are surface traces of conceptual mappings.
Examples (seen in excerpts): ARGUMENT IS WAR ('he attacked every weak point'), TIME IS MONEY ('wasting my time', 'invested time'), orientational HAPPY IS UP / SAD IS DOWN ('feeling up/down').
The authors say TIME IS MONEY is culture-bound, not a necessary way to conceptualise time.
practical_applications: Map the source domain an audience already uses for an abstract topic before inventing a new image.
Use orientational schemas (up/down, in/out, near/far) as layout logic.
limitations: Only excerpts and secondary summaries read this session; claims about thought are inferred mainly from language (see Murphy1996).

title: On metaphoric representation
key_findings: Distinguishes a strong reading of CMT (target understood only via the source) - argued incoherent - from a weaker reading (metaphor shapes a separate target representation), which faces empirical and theoretical problems.

Main objection: metaphoric representations are inferred from linguistic data and then used to explain the same data (circularity); much evidence can be explained by structural similarity between domains.
Replied to by Gibbs (1996) and rejoined by Murphy (1997).
practical_applications: Treat 'people think in metaphor X' as a hypothesis to test with non-linguistic measures, not a fact.
limitations: Read via abstract wording quoted in search results and secondary summaries only.

title: Replication of 'Experiencing physical warmth promotes interpersonal warmth' by Williams & Bargh (2008)
authors: Lynott, D.; Corker, K. S.; Wortman, J.; Connell, L.; Donnellan, M. B.; Lucas, R. E.; O'Brien, K.
key_findings: Three high-powered independent replications of Williams & Bargh (2008, Science) Study 2 (warm vs cold therapeutic pack -> prosocial reward choice), total N = 861.
Effect did not replicate in any lab or in the pooled analysis: no evidence that brief physical warmth increases prosocial choice.
Original studies had small samples (N in the dozens) and large, barely significant effects; Williams wrote a commentary citing conceptual replications.
practical_applications: Do not claim warm colours/props 'make viewers kinder'. Warmth imagery is a code (association), not a proven causal lever.
limitations: Abstract page read; per-lab Ns not read.

title: Does cleanliness influence moral judgments? A direct replication of Schnall, Benton, and Harvey (2008)
authors: Johnson, D. J.; Cheung, F.; Donnellan, M. B.
key_findings: Registered direct replication with >.99 power to detect the original effect sizes: no evidence that cleanliness priming reduces severity of moral judgments.
Schnall replied that the replication data showed a ceiling effect; the dispute became a public case in the replication debate.
practical_applications: Clean/white imagery as 'moral purity' is a cultural code; do not cite it as a behavioural effect.
limitations: Publisher page blocked (403); content from search summaries of the abstract and the reply.

title: Out, Damned Spot: Can the 'Macbeth Effect' Be Replicated?
authors: Earp, B. D.; Everett, J. A. C.; Madva, E. N.; Hamlin, J. K.
key_findings: Direct replications of Zhong & Liljenquist (2006) Study 2 (writing about an unethical deed -> higher desirability of cleansing products) in the UK (N = 153 vs original N = 27), US MTurk and India: no Macbeth effect in any study.
Original Study 2 implied Cohen's d about 1.08 - on the high end even for priming literature; the authors powered for d = 0.5.
An Indian sample (culture with strong purity discourse) also showed no effect.
practical_applications: Moral-cleansing metaphors work as storytelling codes (washing hands = guilt) but are not evidence of automatic behaviour.

title: Evaluating the Replicability of Social Priming Studies
authors: Mac Giolla, E.; Karlsson, S.; Neequaye, D. A.; Bergquist, M.
key_findings: 70 close replications of 49 social-priming findings (search included 'embodied cognition'): 94% had smaller effects than the original; only 17% significant in the original direction.
Replications including an original author: 12/18 significant, pooled d = 0.40 [0.23, 0.58]. Independent teams: 0/52 significant, pooled d = 0.002 [-0.03, 0.03].
Authors: burden of proof is back on advocates of social priming.
practical_applications: Any 'prime the viewer' claim (warm cup -> warm feelings, clean -> moral) should be treated as unproven; design for meaning and clarity instead.
limitations: Social priming broadly; individual embodiment paradigms not broken out in what was read.

title: A pre-registered, multi-lab non-replication of the action-sentence compatibility effect (ACE)
authors: Morey, R. D.; Kaschak, M. P.; Diez-Alamo, A. M.; Glenberg, A. M.; Zwaan, R. A.; Lakens, D.; et al.
key_findings: Pre-registered replication across 18 labs (including the original authors) of the ACE - a flagship embodied-language effect: no lab found a reliable ACE; meta-analytic estimate essentially zero.
Original Glenberg & Kaschak (2002) Exp. 1 (n = 35) had reported a 155 ms effect.
practical_applications: Embodiment claims about language-motor links are weaker than textbooks suggest; keep them as hypotheses.
limitations: Abstract and introduction read; detailed results not read.

title: Metaphorical framing in political discourse through words vs. concepts: a meta-analysis
authors: Brugman, B. C.; Burgers, C.; Vis, B.
key_findings: k = 91 studies, N = 34,783. Metaphorical frames vs literal: overall d = 0.11; beliefs d = 0.29, attitudes d = 0.10, intentions n.s.
Metaphorical-concepts frames (whole message logic, e.g. strategy/conflict frame = POLITICS IS WAR) d = 0.22 vs metaphorical-words frames (single words) d = 0.04.
Publication-bias tests mixed (Begg and Egger significant; trim-and-fill adds one study); journal studies larger (d = 0.13) than grey literature (d = 0.05); effects may have declined over time.
Challenges claims that metaphors are 'home runs of persuasion'.
practical_applications: A metaphor only moves people when it organises the whole message (scenario), not when it is a decorative word.
Expect small effects; never promise persuasion from a single clever image or word.
limitations: Political discourse and verbal stimuli only; not visual ads.

title: Metaphors We Think With: The Role of Metaphor in Reasoning
key_findings: Five experiments: crime framed as a 'beast' vs a 'virus' shifted proposed solutions toward enforcement vs reform (e.g. 74% vs 56% enforcement in Exp. 1; 18-22 point shifts).
A bare word prime without the metaphor had no effect (Exp. 3); the metaphor had no effect when placed at the end of the text (Exp. 5).
Few participants (3-15%) named the metaphor as influential - authors call the effect covert.
practical_applications: Position matters: put the framing metaphor early so it organises what follows.
limitations: Effect later disputed (SteenReijnierseBurgers2014); no literal control condition.

title: When do natural language metaphors influence reasoning? A follow-up study to Thibodeau and Boroditsky (2013)
authors: Steen, G. J.; Reijnierse, W. G.; Burgers, C.
key_findings: Four experiments (N = 253, 259, 252, 1,026) adding a literal control ('crime is a problem'): no metaphorical framing effect in any experiment.
Simply reading about a crime surge shifted preferences toward enforcement regardless of frame.
Proposes boundary conditions: novelty/deliberateness, awareness, topic familiarity, prior opinion; Thibodeau & Boroditsky (2015) re-analysed and argued the effect persists.
practical_applications: Always compare a metaphor version with a plain version before claiming the metaphor did the work.

title: The Persuasive Effects of Metaphor: A Meta-Analysis
key_findings: Meta-analysis of metaphor vs literal messages: metaphors modestly more persuasive; of six theories the 'superior organization' account (metaphor structures the argument) was best supported; seven moderators tested.
A later meta-analysis (studies 2001-2015, cited in search results) reports r = 0.09 [0.06, 0.12].
practical_applications: Use one extended metaphor that organises the argument rather than many decorative ones.
limitations: Abstract-level via repository and citing papers; study count and moderators not verified.

title: Why the Sunny Side Is Up: Associations between Affect and Vertical Position
authors: Meier, B. P.; Robinson, M. D.
key_findings: Positive words evaluated faster at the top of the screen, negative words faster at the bottom; evaluations activated space but space did not activate evaluations (one-directional).
A later replication report (core.ac.uk, not readable here) is described in search results as not supporting the effect.
practical_applications: Up = good is a plausible layout code (rising arrows, hopeful character higher in frame) but its measurable effect is small and contested.
limitations: Abstract via search summaries; replication paper not read (403).

title: Good is up - spatial metaphors in action observation
authors: Gottwald, J. M.; Elsner, B.; Pollatos, O.
key_findings: Three studies (N = 41, 48, 40): watching a neutral cup placed upward vs downward raised gift likelihood and willingness to pay; effects small (r about 0.10-0.16) and inconsistent across measures; 'bad is down' slightly stronger.
Same-lab studies with mostly female German students; not independent replications.
practical_applications: If using vertical movement for valence (product rises into frame), expect at most a small nudge; clarity matters more.

title: A Metaphor-Enriched Social Cognition
authors: Landau, M. J.; Meier, B. P.; Keefer, L. A.
key_findings: Review arguing conceptual metaphor is a distinct mechanism in social cognition; proposes a 'metaphoric transfer strategy' to test whether metaphors shape processing beyond schemas.
Comment by IJzerman & Koole (2011) argued for more bottom-up (perceptual) constraints.
practical_applications: Useful theory map of metaphor-in-social-judgement research - read alongside the replication record (MacGiolla2024).
limitations: Pre-replication-crisis review; many reviewed effects later failed independent replication. Only abstract-level info read.

title: Weapons of Mass Distraction: Optimal Innovation and Pleasure Ratings
authors: Giora, R.; Fein, O.; Kronrod, A.; Elnatan, I.; Shuval, N.; Zur, A.
key_findings: Optimal Innovation Hypothesis: a stimulus that gives a novel response while letting the familiar (salient) one be recovered ('a peace of paper', 'Curl up and Dye') is rated more pleasing than the familiar original, a mere variant, or a pure innovation ('a pill of pepper').
Second most pleasing = the familiar; least = the least familiar. Holds for literal and figurative items and for visual (nonverbal) stimuli (Exp. 6).
Six experiments, Hebrew speakers.
practical_applications: Fresh metaphor = twist a familiar phrase/image so the original is still recognisable; avoid both clichés and riddles.
Pun names, twisted idioms and 'altered familiar objects' are the safe zone.
limitations: Hebrew-speaking student samples; pleasure ratings, not persuasion or recall.

title: The Career of Metaphor
key_findings: Career of metaphor hypothesis: novel metaphors are processed as comparisons (A is like B), and as they become conventional they shift to categorisation; three experiments support a preference for simile form with novel figures.
Estes (2006, cited in search results) argues aptness, not conventionality, better predicts processing.
practical_applications: Novel image metaphors may need a 'like' cue (side-by-side juxtaposition, caption) before audiences accept a fused version.
limitations: Abstract and secondary descriptions only.

title: MIP: A Method for Identifying Metaphorically Used Words in Discourse
key_findings: Four-step procedure: (1) read the whole text; (2) determine lexical units; (3) for each, establish contextual meaning and whether a more basic contemporary meaning exists (more concrete, bodily, precise, historically older) that contrasts with but can be understood in comparison with the context; (4) if yes, mark as metaphorical.
Reports reliability with Cohen's kappa and Cochran's Q; in case studies 70-80% of words are never metaphorical and <5% unanimously metaphorical.
Asks analysts to report texts, readership, resources (dictionary), number of coders and reliability.
practical_applications: Use MIP to audit captions and dialogue: list which words are metaphorical, which are clichés, and whether two metaphors clash.

title: Metaphor in Culture: Universality and Variation
key_findings: Theory of metaphor variation: dimensions of variation (cross-cultural, within-culture), which components of conceptual metaphors vary, and causes (embodiment vs cultural context).

Later Kovecses work (search summaries): AN ANGRY PERSON IS A PRESSURIZED CONTAINER appears in many unrelated languages (English, Japanese, Chinese, Hungarian, Wolof, Zulu, Polish) but its details vary; a 2024 paper notes few systematic contrastive studies.
practical_applications: Generic-level metaphors (pressure, heat, up/down) travel; specific-level details (which container, which animal) must be checked per culture.
limitations: Front matter and secondary summaries only.

title: Pictorial Metaphor in Advertising
key_findings: Applies interaction theory of metaphor to pictures; analyses about thirty ads and billboards; target and source of a pictorial metaphor must be identifiable and the mapping is from source to target.
Forceville later reclassified 'verbo-pictorial' metaphor as a sub-type of multimodal metaphor (target and source rendered in different modes).
practical_applications: When building a visual metaphor, check: what is the target (product/idea)? what is the source? which features map? which mode carries each?
limitations: Book not read; via secondary descriptions and Forceville's own later summaries seen in search results.

title: Multimodal Metaphor
key_findings: Edited volume establishing multimodal metaphor: metaphors whose target and source are rendered exclusively or predominantly in different modes (image, text, sound, gesture, music).
Related chapter 'Pictorial and multimodal metaphor in commercials' (2008) analyses nine commercials.
practical_applications: In clips, a sound (rain SFX) or VO line can be the source domain for a visual target - plan metaphors across modes, not only in the picture.
limitations: Bibliographic and secondary only.

title: The Impact of Verbal Anchoring on Consumer Response to Image Ads
key_findings: Headlines that hint at a pictorial metaphor's meaning raised liking by improving comprehension; headlines that fully spell it out improved comprehension but lowered liking (less pleasure of interpretation).
practical_applications: Caption rule: anchor with a hint, not an explanation. 'Give the key, not the answer'.
limitations: Search summary of the abstract; US student sample (not verified).

title: Encoding/Decoding (orig. 'Encoding and Decoding in the Television Discourse', 1973; repr. in Culture, Media, Language 1980 and The Cultural Studies Reader)
doi_isbn: The Cultural Studies Reader (ed. S. During), Routledge
key_findings: Encoding and decoding are not symmetrical: 'meaning structures 1' (producer) and '2' (audience) may differ; the degree of 'understanding' depends on how far codes are shared.
Naturalised codes: visual signs look 'natural' only because the codes are learned early and widely; even apparently natural visual codes are culture-specific.
Connotation is where ideology works; polysemy is not pluralism - cultures have 'preferred readings'.

Three hypothetical decoding positions: dominant-hegemonic (accepts the preferred reading), negotiated (accepts the frame, applies local exceptions), oppositional (understands but reads it in a contrary frame). Most 'misunderstandings' come from negotiated decodings.
practical_applications: Test with the actual audience: plan the preferred reading, then list likely negotiated and oppositional readings before publishing.
limitations: Read from an archive.org scan of the Cultural Studies Reader chapter (copyright status of upload unclear).

title: Semiotics for Beginners: D.I.Y. Semiotic Analysis - Advice to My Own Students
key_findings: Step list: identify the text (medium, genre, context, purpose); identify signs and the codes within which they mean (textual codes like camerawork, social codes like body language); modality (reality claims); paradigmatic analysis (which alternatives were not chosen; marked vs unmarked; commutation test = imagine swapping one signifier and judge the change); syntagmatic analysis (sequence and spatial arrangement); rhetorical tropes; intertextuality; anchorage; ideology - what reality the text constructs and how it naturalises it.
Recommends comparing paired texts rather than analysing one text alone.
practical_applications: Basis for the studio's step-by-step semiotic audit (section 6).
limitations: Online teaching text, undated in page read; expert but not peer-reviewed.

title: A Theory of Semiotics (Introduction excerpt)
doi_isbn: Indiana University Press (Eng. of Trattato di semiotica generale, 1975)
key_findings: Semiotics as a unified theory of signification (theory of codes) and communication (theory of sign production); replaces 'sign' with 'sign-function' - a correlation posited by social convention.
'Theory of the lie': semiotics studies everything that can be used to lie - if something cannot be used to lie it cannot be used to tell the truth.
Revisits Peirce's icon/index/symbol typology as a typology of modes of sign production; Hall1973 cites Eco: iconic signs look like objects because they reproduce the codes of perception.
Aberrant decoding (Eco 1965/1972, via secondary sources): a message encoded in one code is decoded with another.
practical_applications: Every image can 'lie' - including unintentionally - so meaning must be checked, not assumed from intent.
limitations: Introduction excerpt only; aberrant decoding from secondary sources.

title: Mythologies (incl. 'Myth Today')
doi_isbn: Editions du Seuil, Paris; Eng. trans. A. Lavers 1972
key_findings: 'Myth Today': myth is a second-order semiological system - a complete sign of the first system becomes a mere signifier in the second (excerpt read).

Paris Match cover (no. 326, 1955): denoted 'a young Black soldier in French uniform saluting'; mythic signification 'France is a great empire, all her sons serve her' - which naturalises colonialism (via secondary summaries).
practical_applications: Ask of every image: what 'obvious, natural' message rides on top of the literal one, and who benefits from it seeming natural?
limitations: Only a short excerpt and secondary summaries read; not the full essay.

title: Meaning Matters: Polysemy in Advertising
authors: Puntoni, S.; Schroeder, J. E.; Ritson, M.
key_findings: Advertising polysemy = multiple interpretations of one message; cross-disciplinary review (psychology, semiotics, literary theory); introduces 'purposeful polysemy' (strategic ambiguity) and a framework with research propositions.
practical_applications: Decide on purpose whether an image should have one reading (anchor it) or several (purposeful polysemy) - and check that none of the extra readings are harmful.
limitations: Abstract only.

title: Creating Brand Names with Meaning: The Use of Sound Symbolism
key_findings: Fictitious brand names varying by one sound: front vowels (i, e) conveyed smaller, lighter, faster, sharper, milder, more feminine; back vowels (o, u) the opposite; voiceless consonants rated smaller, sharper, faster (as reported by citing papers).
practical_applications: Name/wordmark sound should fit the product's meaning (light titanium frame vs heavy bold acetate).
limitations: English-speaking samples; findings via citing papers; Thai tonal phonology untested.

title: Rapid and dynamic processing of face pareidolia in the human brain
authors: Wardle, S. G.; Taubert, J.; Teichmann, L.; Baker, C. I.
key_findings: fMRI + MEG: illusory faces in objects are represented in face-selective cortex and initially resemble real faces, but within ~250 ms become equivalent to ordinary objects.
Interpreted as a broadly tuned face-detection mechanism that favours sensitivity over selectivity (many false alarms); pareidolia also shown in macaques.
practical_applications: Viewers will see faces in any face-like arrangement (two dots + curve) - check props, backgrounds and AI images for accidental faces, especially in 'faceless' character art.

title: This Car is (Technically) Red: Beliefs about Colors in Thailand
key_findings: Day colours: Sun red, Mon yellow, Tue pink, Wed green, Thu orange, Fri purple (as listed here; other sources give Fri light blue and Sat purple), Wednesday night (Rahu) black; traced to Hindu planetary myth.
Brahma's three qualities: purity = white, movement = red, weight = black; Buddha images gilded or white to signify purity.
Birth-day colour taboos (e.g. Tuesday-born avoid yellow and white); 'This car is red' stickers to neutralise an unlucky colour; beliefs described as personal, not a society-wide standard.
practical_applications: Use day/birth colours as optional, playful cultural codes; never as claims of luck in ads.
limitations: Popular article by a state-linked foundation; day list differs from other sources (Friday/Saturday).

title: Mapping Metaphor: The 'Heart' and 'Face' of Thai Nirat
doi_isbn: Excellent Language & Linguistics Dissertation Repository (ELLDR), Newcastle University, Vol. 4
key_findings: Analyses heart (jai) and face (naa) metaphors in two Thai nirat (travel poems) using Gricean pragmatics, CMT and Matisoff's psycho-collocations.
'Heart' dominated as a source domain; most compounds were adjectives; both conventional and novel metaphors present; N+N compounds not predicted by prior literature.
Calls for native-speaker judgement tasks.
practical_applications: Thai jai-compounds are mostly conventional (dead) metaphors - fresh Thai metaphors must go beyond them.
limitations: Undergraduate dissertation; two poems only.

title: Marketing Semiotics: Signs, Strategies, and Brand Value
key_findings: Argues brand equity depends on managing brand meanings; applies structural semiotics to verbal, visual and spatial brand sign systems; case-based chapters (World of Goods, Consumer Brandscape, Brand Discourse, Consumer Space).
practical_applications: Map a brand's codes (what category conventions it follows or breaks) before redesigning assets.
limitations: Publisher/catalogue description only; practitioner-academic author with a consultancy.

title: The Man Behind the FedEx Logo (interview with Lindon Leader)
key_findings: Leader (Landor, 1994) noticed 'a hint of an arrow' between E and x and redrew the letterforms so it looked natural; the arrow was meant to stand for speed and precision.
He calls it 'a hidden bonus' - the logo works whether or not you see it; Landor rejected the PR agency's idea of highlighting the arrow.
practical_applications: Hidden secondary signs should be a bonus layer, never required for the main message.
limitations: Designer's own account; no audience data.

title: Draw Ketchup / Heinz Draw Ketchup (D&AD awards archive)
key_findings: Anonymous social experiment asking people to 'draw ketchup': D&AD reports 97% drew Heinz; drawings used as OOH, print, social and TV; agency entries claim a sales lift (self-reported, not verified).
practical_applications: Evidence that a brand's shape (bottle, label keystone) can become the category icon - a distinctive asset owned at the level of the sign.
limitations: Award-entry data, agency self-report; sample method not disclosed.

title: Smoking Kid - A Personal Message to the Smokers (Jay Chiat Awards 2013 case)
authors: Thai Health Promotion Foundation; Ogilvy & Mather Thailand
key_findings: Child actors asked adult smokers for a light; smokers lectured them; kids handed a note: 'You worry about me, but why not about yourself?' + 1600 Quitline.
Built on a Thai cultural code: hierarchical respect - elders must set an example and teach children.

Reported: completed calls rose from avg 7,057/month (Jan-May) to 11,461 in June (+62%); Jul-Nov avg 9,321 (+32%); cost ~$5,000 with no media spend; >5 million views in 10 days; earned media valued at USD 3.2 million (self-reported).
practical_applications: A role reversal inside a known cultural code (child teaches adult) creates the 'incongruity' that makes a message land.
limitations: Award case written by the agency/client; earned-media values self-reported.

title: Burberry apologizes for noose hoodie after model complains at London Fashion Week
key_findings: 17 Feb 2019: hoodie with a knotted rope around the neck resembling a noose; designer said it drew on a nautical theme.
Model Liz Kennedy: 'Suicide is not fashion'; raised suicide and lynching history; said concerns raised before the show were not acted on.
CEO apologised 'for the distress'; item and all images removed from the collection.
practical_applications: Intent (nautical) does not control decoding: a rope loop at the neck/head reads as a noose.
limitations: News report.

title: Thai university apologizes for Hitler banner
key_findings: July 2013: freshman art students at Chulalongkorn painted a graduation billboard showing Hitler giving a Nazi salute beside Batman, Captain America, Hulk and Iron Man.
Students: 'superheroes protecting the world'; dean: good and bad coexist, Hitler in grayscale as a 'conceptual paradox'; formal apology after Simon Wiesenthal Center criticism; banner removed.
AP notes Thai school history curriculum mentions the Holocaust little or not at all.
practical_applications: A symbol's meaning in a local code (pop 'villain/strongman') differs from its global meaning (genocide) - global platforms decode globally.
limitations: News report.

title: Dunkin' Donuts Thailand 'Charcoal Donut' blackface ad (news coverage)
authors: Multiple outlets (AP via CBS/Global News/SCMP; Bangkok Post)
key_findings: Aug 2013: Thai franchise ad showed a woman in blackface with bright pink lips holding a bitten black donut; HRW called it 'bizarre and racist'.
Thai franchise CEO initially defended it (reported as 'paranoid American thinking') and said sales rose ~50%; US parent apologised and pulled the spot.
Coverage noted the ad did not ruffle many in Thailand, where ads commonly use racial stereotypes.
practical_applications: Same sign, two decoding communities: a local 'novelty/colour' joke reads globally as racist caricature.
limitations: Search-result summaries of several news reports; full articles not read (paywall/403).

title: H&M apologises for 'coolest monkey in the jungle' hoodie ad (news coverage)
key_findings: Jan 2018: online product image of a Black child wearing a hoodie reading 'coolest monkey in the jungle'; image removed and apology issued; The Weeknd ended his collaboration; second apology 'we have got this wrong'.
practical_applications: Text + image anchorage can create a meaning neither has alone; check every text-on-person combination.
limitations: Search-result summaries.

title: Guidelines for Selecting or Modifying Logos
authors: Henderson, P. W.; Cote, J. A.
key_findings: (As summarised by Kim & Lim 2019) Logo design characteristics (active, balance, cohesive, complex, depth, organic, parallel, proportion, repetition, representative, round, symmetric) were related to correct recognition, false recognition, affect and familiar meaning.
Three underlying design dimensions: elaborateness (complexity, activeness, depth), naturalness (representative, organic) and harmony (symmetry + balance).

Guidelines by objective: high-recognition logos = very natural, very harmonious, moderately elaborate; low-investment logos = less natural, very harmonious, moderately elaborate; high-image logos = moderately natural, very harmonious, moderately elaborate.
Figurative logos depicting familiar objects need less learning and are recognised more easily than abstract ones.
practical_applications: Brief a new mark as 'harmonious + moderately elaborate'; choose figurative/natural when there is little media budget to teach an abstract mark.
limitations: Full text not read this session; findings come from Kim & Lim (2019) review footnotes.

US student sample, black-and-white logos, late-1990s stimuli; later cross-national work (Henderson et al. 2003; van der Lans et al. 2009) reportedly supports the three dimensions but colour/motion were not tested.

title: Universal Patterns in Color-Emotion Associations Are Further Shaped by Linguistic and Geographic Proximity
key_findings: Psychological Science 31(10):1245-1260. 4,598 participants, 30 nations, 22 languages, 20 emotion concepts × 12 colour terms.
Strong cross-national similarity (mean r = .88) plus nation-specific differences, larger similarity for linguistically/geographically close nations.
practical_applications: Colour-emotion associations are largely shared but locally tuned: check Thai associations; colour terms, not rendered colours, were tested.
limitations: Specific colour-emotion pairs not read; colour words not images; Thailand participation not confirmed.

title: A Review of Studies in Heart or Jai Metaphor in Thai Language
key_findings: Manutsat Paritat: Journal of Humanities 45(2), 68-85. Jai (heart) metaphors fall into four groups: heart as person, object, space, container; central to everyday Thai emotion talk.
practical_applications: Visual metaphors for Thai emotion (a 'cool' or 'wide' heart) can be drawn from these mappings.
limitations: Abstract only; DOI shown on page looked malformed, omitted.

title: Peirce's Theory of Signs
authors: (SEP entry; author not captured in the fetched text)
key_findings: A sign is determined by an Object and produces an effect (interpretant) in a person; it signifies only as it is interpreted.
Icon = signifies by shared quality (portrait, diagram); index = existential/causal link (smoke-fire, weathercock, pointing finger); symbol = convention/habit/law (words, traffic lights).
Peirce came to see pure icons and indices as rare; most signs mix iconic, indexical and symbolic features (hypo-icon, sub-index).
Later typologies (10 and 66 classes) are uncertain even for Peirce and are disputed by scholars.
practical_applications: Classify every visual element by HOW it carries meaning: icons travel across cultures best, symbols least.
An index (steam from a cup, footprints, worn edges) shows a cause and needs little caption; a symbol needs shared convention or a caption.
limitations: Author and revision date not captured.
Only the sections on the triad and typologies were summarised.

title: Rhetoric of the Image (in Image-Music-Text, trans. S. Heath)
key_findings: Analyses a Panzani pasta ad as three messages: a linguistic message, a coded iconic (symbolic/connoted) message and a non-coded iconic (literal/denoted) message; the literal message supports the symbolic one.

Connoted signs: the half-open string bag spilling provisions = 'return from the market' with the euphoric values of freshness and domestic preparation; tomato, pepper and the poster's yellow-green-red = 'Italianicity', a specifically French knowledge - 'an Italian would barely perceive' it; the name Panzani itself connotes Italianicity by assonance.

All images are polysemous ('a floating chain of signifieds'); text relates to image by anchorage (fixes the reading, has a repressive value; most frequent, common in press photographs and advertisements) or relay (text and image complementary, unity at the level of the story; seen particularly in cartoons and comic strips).
practical_applications: Captions in our posts are anchorage: write them to close off unwanted readings.
Mint & Tao speech bubbles are relay: text carries the plot the image cannot.
limitations: Read in Trachtenberg (ed.) Classic Essays on Photography (1980), Heath translation; essay first published 1964.
Interpretive/theoretical, not empirical.

title: Visual Rhetoric in Advertising: Text-Interpretive, Experimental, and Reader-Response Analyses
authors: McQuarrie, E. F.; Mick, D. G.
key_findings: Visual figures tested (rhyme, antithesis, metaphor, pun) produced more elaboration and more favourable ad attitude without lower comprehension.
Reader-response interviews matched the text-based analysis.
Effects of visual tropes (metaphor, pun) diminished or disappeared for people lacking the cultural competency to read the (American) ads.
practical_applications: Visual metaphor helps only when the audience shares the code: for foreign tourists, prefer schemes or very common metaphors.
limitations: Abstract only; US ads and samples; a 2003 follow-up (JCR 29(4)) examined directed vs incidental exposure (not read).

title: Beyond Visual Metaphor: A New Typology of Visual Rhetoric in Advertising
authors: Phillips, B. J.; McQuarrie, E. F.
key_findings: Typology built from properties of pictures: visual structure (juxtaposition, fusion, replacement) x meaning operation (connection, comparison) per Lagerwerf2023's summary.
Ordered by complexity: juxtaposition < fusion < replacement (as commonly summarised).
A later student study (search snippet, source not identified) reported juxtaposition prompted more elaboration and fusion was hardest to comprehend.
practical_applications: Template for product metaphors: side-by-side (juxtaposition) for broad audiences; fused object for engaged followers; replacement only with strong context.
limitations: Original article not read; typology described via secondary sources (Lagerwerf2023, a 2018 International Journal of Advertising extension at the URL).
'Connection/comparison' categories confirmed only through Lagerwerf2023's text.

title: Conceptual similarity and visual metaphor: effects on viewing times, appreciation, and recall
authors: Lagerwerf, L.; van Mulken, M.; Lagerwerf, J. B.
key_findings: Three experiments (N=65, 73, 73) with 27 juxtaposed object pairs: hyponyms (same kind), visual comparisons (metaphors), unrelated.
Hyponyms identified fastest and liked most; metaphors next; unrelated last.
Longer exposure did not change preference; recall lowest for unrelated pairs; 5 s exposure improved recall.
Fluency theory explained appreciation better than the 'pleasure of solving' view; the inverted U was not found.
practical_applications: In fast-scrolling feeds, easy-to-process pairings win liking; save puzzling metaphors for content people stop to read.
limitations: About 100k of 121k characters read; lab stimuli, not real ads; Dutch-context samples; no culture comparison.

title: The lotus in Buddhism (100 Flowers exhibition)
authors: Asian Art Museum of San Francisco
key_findings: Asian Art Museum: the lotus is one of the most important and recognised Buddhist symbols across all Buddhist cultures; it symbolises purity, 'spontaneous' generation, faithfulness and spiritual awakening.
Thai details (bua luang, merit-making, funeral use) come from earlier search summaries of Thai press, not from this page.
practical_applications: Lotus is safe and positive for Thai audiences in calm/wellness contexts; avoid on feet, floors, trash, or comic contexts.
limitations: Short museum page; Thai-specific uses not verified here.

title: (Number nine in Thai creative culture) - Journal of Humanities, Naresuan University
key_findings: Number nine is significantly applied in Thai 'creative' culture, linked to astrology/sacredness and its homophone (kao ~ 'step forward' = progress).
Popular sources add: nine monks at blessings, nine auspicious desserts, record lucky-licence-plate auctions (Bangkok Post: ~45m baht).
practical_applications: 9 is a positive number in Thai promos (e.g. 9.9 campaigns, 99 baht) - meaning 'progress'.
limitations: PDF text garbled; title/authors not captured; methods unverified.

title: Thailand: One-year period of mourning declared
authors: Al Jazeera (and other news reports in the same search)
key_findings: After King Bhumibol's death (13 Oct 2016) the government declared one year of mourning; black and white worn nationwide; black clothing shortages; reports say other subdued colours were later accepted.
practical_applications: Use monochrome/black-white for condolence posts; pause festive palettes during national mourning.
limitations: News summaries; exact official wording not read.

title: The bouba/kiki effect is robust across cultures and writing systems
authors: Aleksandra Ćwiek et al. (incl. Marcus Perlman)
key_findings: 917 speakers of 25 languages (9 families, 10 writing systems): strong overall evidence for the bouba/kiki effect; bouba more consistent than kiki; largely independent of orthography.
practical_applications: Round shapes match soft-sounding names and voices; pair round mascots with soft names/voices, spiky ones with sharp.
limitations: Abstract and press; whether Thai was among the languages not confirmed.
